opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think those reports are really informative, and I don't read them as "RL doesn't work." I read them as "RL amplifies what's already there." Reinforcement learning on language models is mostly a process of selection and sharpening. The model generates a bunch of attempts, some get rewarded, and you push probability mass toward those. That only works if the model is already producing correct, or at least partially correct, reasoning some reasonable fraction of the time. If the base model almost never stumbles onto a good chain of thought, there's no signal. You're sampling, getting zero reward, and the gradient has nothing to grab onto.

So with a weaker model you can end up in a regime where the reward is just too sparse. Or you get the other failure mode: the model finds some cheap trick to game the reward, because that's the easiest thing within its reach, rather than learning to reason more carefully. A stronger model has a richer repertoire of behaviors to draw on: things like backtracking, checking its work, trying a different approach. RL can then find and reinforce those. A weaker model may just not have those latent behaviors in a usable form.

That's why I think of pre-training and RL as complementary rather than competing. Pre-training builds up the raw capability and the space of behaviors the model can express. RL then shapes which of those behaviors it actually uses and how persistently it uses them. If the foundation isn't there, RL doesn't have much to work with.

I'd also add a caveat: some of those negative results are partly about recipe. The details matter a lot: how you design the reward, the curriculum of problems, making sure tasks are hard enough to be interesting but not so hard that success is vanishingly rare, keeping the training stable. Smaller labs or academic groups trying this early on often didn't have all of those pieces dialed in. So some failures were genuinely about model capability, and some were about it being a hard engineering problem. Over time, as people figured out better recipes, you've seen RL start to work on smaller models too, especially when you distill from a stronger reasoning model first to give the small model a good starting point. That fits the same picture. You're giving it the behaviors first, and then RL can sharpen them.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts pre-training and reinforcement learning as complementary, but does not compare RL’s difficulty with the earlier difficulty of making large-scale pretraining work reliably.

r002.rationale: It lists possible RL failure causes, but does not explain that fixing one fault may show no improvement while other faults remain.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the more interesting empirical questions right now, and I'd interpret those reports pretty carefully rather than drawing a sweeping conclusion from them.

The first thing I'd say is that RL on language models is really sensitive to the base model having enough latent capability for the reward signal to get any purchase. If you're doing RL with verifiable rewards on math or code, you need the model to sometimes get the answer right in the first place. If your pass rate on the problem distribution is essentially zero, you have no positive examples, there's no gradient to speak of, and the whole thing just doesn't move. So when people say "we tried RL on a small model and it didn't work," a lot of the time what they're actually observing is that the prior was too weak for the problems they chose. That's less a statement about RL and more a statement about the mismatch between the task difficulty and the model's starting point. If you curate problems that sit right at the edge of what the small model can do, you tend to see it learn something.

The second thing is that RL amplifies whatever is already there. The way I think about it is that pretraining gives you this broad distribution over behaviours, and RL is sharpening and reweighting that distribution toward the ones that get rewarded. It's much less about teaching something genuinely new from scratch. So a larger model has a richer set of behaviours to select from, and you see these dramatic gains, the long chains of reasoning, the self-verification, backtracking and so on. A smaller model just has fewer of those behaviours available in the first place, so the ceiling is lower and you can hit it fast, or you get a kind of collapse where the model finds one narrow strategy and overfits to it.

Third, and I think this is underappreciated, RL is just finicky to get right at an engineering level. The details matter enormously: how you handle the KL constraint, the reward normalisation, the batch sizes, how long your rollouts are, whether the reward is actually verifying the thing you care about or something exploitable. A lot of academic groups are working with small compute budgets, and RL eats compute because you're generating a lot of samples that you then throw away. So failures in that setting can just be undertuned runs rather than a fundamental limit.

Where I'd be a bit humble is that I don't think we have a clean scaling law for this yet. With pretraining we have a very good sense of what you get for a given amount of compute and data. With RL the picture is murkier. It clearly works at the frontier, and there's some evidence that you can distill the resulting reasoning behaviours down into smaller models through supervised fine-tuning on the traces, which suggests the knowledge can live in a small model even if small models struggle to discover it through RL on their own. That distinction, between what a model can represent and what it can discover under exploration, is I think the crux of it.

So my overall take is: these reports are real, they're informative, but the right reading is "RL has a capability floor below which exploration doesn't find the signal," not "RL doesn't work on small models." And I'd expect that floor to come down over time as people get better at curriculum design and reward shaping.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite hard to interpret a negative result there, because reinforcement learning depends a lot on what the model can already do. If the model occasionally produces a good solution, then reinforcement learning has something to work with: you can reward that solution and make it more likely. But if the model never produces anything that gets reward, there’s very little signal to learn from.

So you can imagine the same setup failing on a weaker model and working on a stronger one, without there being any contradiction. The stronger model might just cross the threshold where it can explore useful solutions often enough to improve.

I’d want to know what tasks they were using, how they were giving reward, and whether the starting model had any success on those tasks. A failure is evidence about that particular setup. It’s much harder to turn it into a general conclusion about whether reinforcement learning works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those reports are hard to interpret without knowing exactly what people tried. Reinforcement learning can be quite sensitive to the setup: how you generate problems, how you score answers, and how much exploration you allow. So a negative result doesn’t necessarily tell you that the model is fundamentally incapable of benefiting from it.

But there is a real capability question underneath that. If the model occasionally produces a good solution, reinforcement learning has something to reinforce. If it almost never gets anywhere near a good solution, then a sparse reward signal is going to be much less useful. You might need easier problems, a curriculum, or some other way of getting learning started.

So I’d distinguish ‘this particular recipe didn’t work at this scale’ from ‘reinforcement learning doesn’t work at this scale.’ The first is useful evidence, but it’s a much narrower claim than the second.
